strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing genuine scalability challenges in emerging Agent Web ecosystems with Model Context Protocol
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (MCP-Universe, MCP-Mark) with diverse domains and extensive robustness analysis (noise, scalability, generalization)
Strong empirical results showing that small fine-tuned router (8B params) outperforms much larger generalist models (GPT-4o: 47.41%, Gemini-2.5-Pro: 49.79% vs. proposed: 53.44%)
Practical system design with Light Routing Agent that elegantly decouples routing logic from tool definitions, enabling seamless integration and generalization to agent selection (91.6% accuracy)
Scalable data synthesis approach using LLM-driven trajectory generation without requiring real API access, enabling efficient training data expansion from 627 to 2,005 tools
Clear presentation with effective motivation figures and comprehensive appendices documenting mutation taxonomies and benchmark details
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Individual components (cosine-similarity graphs, LLM-based mutation, random walk sampling, LoRA fine-tuning) are well-established; their combination is incremental without conceptual innovation

Critical dependency on synthetic data validity: All 15,092 training samples are LLM-generated without validation against real agent interactions; lacks quality analysis, diversity metrics, or bias assessment; creates distribution shift and potential data leakage risks

Weak experimental baselines: Embedding-based retrieval appears strawman-like (simple cosine similarity); ReAct baseline uses Gemini-2.5-Pro which may not be optimized for routing; missing comparisons with recent routing methods cited in related work

Agent routing generalization demonstrated on only 156 author-created synthetic test samples without independent validation or inter-annotator agreement metrics; claims of 'seamless generalization' and 'cross-domain transferability' exceed evidence

Overstated scalability: Paper claims 'millions of tools' but only tests ~2,000; no experiments at 10K+; training data (15K samples for 2K tools) scalability undemonstrated; 'exceptional stability' shown only in constrained single-server setting

Insufficient component analysis: Missing ablations on graph construction (mutation vs. similarity edges), which mutation types help most, sensitivity to similarity threshold τ=0.82, and what patterns the router learns through feature analysis

Synthetic data validity unaddressed: No comparison with real trajectories, no human evaluation of synthetic quality, no distribution analysis showing GPT-4o synthesized trajectories match real agent behavior; entire evaluation at risk from distribution shift

Reproducibility concerns: Approach entirely dependent on GPT-4o API for trajectory synthesis; MCP tool selection process under-specified; agent bank creation vague; no code/data availability mentioned; resource constraints limit to Qwen3-8B only

Limited analysis of why router outperforms large models: Paper attributes this to 'fine-grained discrimination' without rigorous investigation; could reflect that LLMs aren't optimized for routing rather than superiority of synthetic training

No statistical significance testing beyond average@5; lacks confidence intervals and error analysis; no investigation of failure modes or systematic errors; insufficient discussion of handling dynamic ecosystems with frequently added tools

strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem: tool/agent selection at scale in emerging MCP ecosystems
Comprehensive experimental analysis including scalability, robustness, cross-domain generalization, and ablations
Strong empirical results on established benchmarks (53.44% vs 49.79% on MCP-Universe)
Interesting transfer from tool routing to agent routing (91.6% on agent benchmark) without retraining
Generally clear presentation with effective visual contrasts between paradigms
weaknesses: Unfair baseline comparison: router trained on 15,092 samples synthesized by GPT-4o then compared against GPT-4o itself; missing control experiments with fine-tuned baselines on same training data
Limited novelty: primarily an engineering combination of established techniques (graph-based selection, LLM trajectory synthesis, mutation operators); Light Routing Agent is a trivial wrapper

Critical reproducibility gaps: LLM-generated training data lacks human validation; many design choices (τ=0.82 threshold, mutation operator selection, random walk parameters) are unjustified and not ablated
Small test sets undermine claims: agent routing evaluated on only 156 samples; no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or p-values reported despite small sample sizes
Evaluation limited to single metric (accuracy) with no error analysis, breakdown by tool/domain categories, or investigation of failure modes
Unvalidated circular dependency: using GPT-4o-generated data to train a router that outperforms GPT-4o confounds data advantage with architectural superiority
Scalability claims unsupported: tested on ~2,000 tools only; no complexity analysis; real agent webs could require orders of magnitude more candidates
Missing critical methodological details: tool dependencies/constraints handling, out-of-distribution generalization (entirely new tools), computational costs, cross-domain evaluation
Questionable novelty of 'history-aware' framing: incorporating dialogue history in multi-turn reasoning is standard; no clear explanation of what is novel beyond baseline approaches
Overclaimed results: 'universal orchestration in open-ended ecosystems' claimed but supported only by two benchmarks with limited scope

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing timely challenges in the Agent Web and MCP ecosystem scaling
Strong empirical results: 53.44% on MCP-Universe and 60% on MCP-Mark, outperforming larger generalist models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) with a smaller 8B specialized router
Exceptional generalization to agent routing (91.6% accuracy) despite training exclusively on tool data, demonstrating transfer of fundamental capability matching logic
Comprehensive robustness evaluation including multi-server scalability, noise resilience from both external tools and synthesized mutations, with large performance gaps vs. baselines (56% vs. 28-32%)
Clear ablation study quantifying the value of history-aware routing (5-8% improvements across benchmarks)
Practical and elegant system design with the Light Routing Agent requiring minimal interface (router invocation + execution tools)
Evaluation across multiple real-world benchmarks (MCP-Universe with 6 domains, MCP-Mark with 5 real tool environments)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: individual components (semantic similarity graphs, random walk sampling, multi-agent trajectory synthesis) are well-established; the contribution is primarily engineering integration rather than methodological innovation

Critical concern with trajectory synthesis: entire pipeline relies on LLM-simulated trajectories without validation against real tool behavior, success patterns, or failure modes; no analysis of synthesis quality or alignment with reality

Insufficient training data analysis: no breakdown by mutation type or domain, no quality checks on synthesized 15,092 samples, no evidence that router learns generalizable patterns vs. exploiting synthesis artifacts (e.g., always-succeeding simulated tools)

Experimental design bias: fixing downstream execution to Gemini-2.5-Pro may artificially favor the router trained on LLM simulations; missing comparisons with recent history-aware (Yang et al., 2024a; Patel et al., 2025) and graph-based routing methods (Du et al., 2025c; Zhang et al., 2024)

Limited analysis of history mechanism: ablation confirms history helps but provides no insight into learned patterns, failure cases, or representation of long histories (max 32K tokens)
Missing ablations: similarity threshold τ=0.82 'empirically set' without justification; LoRA rank=8 not ablated; Qwen3-8B choice not justified; DFS vs. BFS traversal rationale unexplained
Agent routing evaluation limited to 156 synthetically-generated samples without real-world agent composition scenarios or evidence of generalization beyond training distribution
No statistical significance testing or confidence intervals reported; results only shown as avg@5
Reproducibility concerns: GPT-4o-based mutation process lacks detail; no mention of code/data release; trajectory synthesis prompts incompletely specified

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical challenges in emerging MCP-based agent ecosystems with strong empirical results (53.44% on MCP-Universe, outperforming GPT-4o and Gemini-2.5-Pro)

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including ablation studies, robustness analysis, and human validation of synthetic data quality (Cohen's κ = 0.93); results reported with standard deviations across 5 runs
Thoughtful system design combining graph-based expansion, self-evolutionary mutation, and multi-agent trajectory synthesis for creating training supervision from LLM-generated trajectories
Promising cross-domain transfer from tool routing to agent selection (91.6% accuracy) suggesting learned capability-matching patterns generalize within the ecosystem
Demonstrated robustness to noise and scaling within MCP benchmarks with minimal performance degradation under adverse conditions
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: self-evolutionary mutation and multi-agent trajectory synthesis build directly on prior work (Self-Evolve, Liu et al. 2024, Wang et al. 2025); primary contribution is combining existing techniques rather than novel methods

Significant disconnect between claims and evaluation scope: paper claims applicability to 'Agent Web' and 'open-ended ecosystems' but evaluation is limited to MCP benchmarks; agent routing validated on only 156 test samples

Methodological rigor concerns: DFS-style traversal algorithm poorly explained (seed selection, stopping criteria undefined), similarity threshold τ=0.82 appears arbitrary without sensitivity analysis, history truncation mechanism unclear despite 32,768 token max sequence

Overstated scalability claims: tested on ~2,000 tools (not truly massive), no evaluation on 10k+ candidate spaces, claims about 'web-scale' and 'millions of agents' unvalidated; trained only on 8B model due to resource constraints

Generalization claims exceed evidence: tool→agent transfer occurs within MCP ecosystem where both are capability-matching tasks; true cross-domain generalization to non-MCP ecosystems remains unvalidated

Synthetic data validation incomplete: while κ=0.93 validates LLM labels against humans on 100 trajectories, doesn't guarantee coverage of diverse routing scenarios or verify distribution matches real deployments; potential data leakage risk unexplored

Missing critical analyses: no error breakdown of failure modes, no sensitivity to history length or mutation operator importance, no learning curves, computational costs (training time/inference latency) not discussed

Incomplete experimental details: agent collection methodology sparse ('40 mainstream agents' undefined), benchmark construction for 156 agent routing samples unclear, explanation missing for cases where query-only embeddings outperform query+history approaches

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real scalability bottlenecks in emerging Agent Web ecosystems
Strong empirical results consistently outperforming generalist LLMs (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) and embedding baselines across multiple benchmarks
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple benchmarks, diverse baselines, thoughtful ablations, robustness analysis under noise/scalability conditions, and variance reporting across 5 runs
Interesting cross-domain generalization from tool routing to agent routing achieving 91.6% accuracy, suggesting learning of abstract capability-matching patterns
Good reproducibility practices with detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, and code availability commitment
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: self-evolutionary mutation borrowed directly from prior work, graph construction standard, multi-agent synthesis combines existing approaches, Light Routing Agent is minimal wrapper—contribution is primarily engineering combination rather than methodological innovation

Critical reliance on LLM-generated synthetic training data without real API execution, with human validation only on 100 samples (1% of 15K training set); no analysis of distribution gap between simulated trajectories and real user interactions

Generalization claims significantly overstated: 'Agent Web' scale with only 2,005 tools and 156 agent test samples is modest; agent evaluation limited to single benchmark family (MCP); no cross-domain or real-world agent orchestration scenarios tested

Substantial methodological gaps: similarity threshold τ=0.82 'empirically set' without sensitivity analysis; random-walk sampling underspecified; mutation selection random without ablating individual types; trajectory generation mechanisms vague

Experimental limitations: single model architecture (Qwen3-8B LoRA) due to computational constraints limiting generalization assessment; agent benchmark created by authors with limited external validation; no comparisons with recent dense retrieval or hybrid approaches beyond appendix

History-aware modeling underexplored: modest improvements (5-8%) with straightforward context concatenation; no analysis of learned patterns or comparison with alternative history incorporation methods; 'sequential dependency' and 'error recovery' claimed but not demonstrated
Missing ablations and analysis: no individual ablation on mutation types, graph structure, or sampling strategy; no trajectory diversity analysis; no sensitivity studies on hyperparameters
Practical deployment concerns unaddressed: training requires GPT-4o API access (cost/availability); execution tool implementation unclear; no latency or cost analysis provided

strengths: Well-motivated problem in emerging MCP/Agent Web ecosystems with clear articulation of limitations in existing approaches (scalability, history-awareness)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with proper ablations, robustness testing (noise, scalability), and reporting of standard deviations across 5 runs
Strong empirical results showing specialized 8B router outperforming large models (GPT-4o, Gemini-2.5-Pro) by substantial margins (53.44% vs 49.79% on MCP-Universe)
Exceptional cross-domain generalization: router trained on tools achieves 91.67% on agent routing without additional fine-tuning, demonstrating learning of abstract capability matching
Practical Light Routing Agent design elegantly decouples routing from task execution via minimal interface, enabling seamless integration into existing pipelines
Manual validation of synthetic trajectories (κ=0.93) demonstrates data quality; robust performance under noise injection and candidate space expansion
Thorough documentation with extensive appendices including mutation taxonomies, prompts, and standardized agent definitions
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: primarily combines existing techniques (graph-based representation, self-evolutionary mutation from prior work, standard LLM-based trajectory synthesis) without fundamental methodological innovation

Synthetic data generalization concerns: all training data generated by LLMs without real API execution; human validation only on 100 samples; no analysis of sim-to-real gap or execution-specific failure modes

Scope limitations: evaluated only on tool/agent selection (straightforward retrieval tasks); claims of 'universal orchestration' not proportional to narrow evaluation scope; agent benchmark newly constructed (156 samples) rather than established

Unfair baseline comparisons: generalist models (GPT-4o, Gemini) not designed for routing; simple embedding baselines used instead of modern dense retrieval or learning-to-rank methods; specialized router advantage somewhat expected

Incomplete scalability analysis: tested only on ~2,000 tools; minimal degradation (0.4%) doesn't establish true 'web-scale' capability; no complexity analysis for random walk sampling on massive graphs

Unjustified technical choices: similarity threshold τ=0.82 lacks ablation; no justification for random walk over alternative subset selection; mutation strategy effectiveness not analyzed
Reproducibility gaps: code URL missing, multi-agent synthesis framework vaguely described, hyperparameter choices (LoRA rank, learning rate) lack justification
Overstated claims relative to evidence: 'critical properties for Agent Web', 'universal orchestration', 'seamless generalization' not fully supported by evaluation scope
Missing error analysis: no failure case discussion, no examples of router weaknesses, no analysis of what model learns beyond retrieval, insufficient exploration of when/why history helps
